A cousin of Crazy Horse, this Oglala Sioux fought at the battle of Little Bighorn as a teenager. However, at the age of nine he had had a powerful vision that set him on the path to being a holy man with the sacred mission of preserving the purity of Sioux traditions. By 1947 he was indeed the last living Sioux to possess full knowledge of the metaphysics and practices of the Sioux religion. So, he agreed to relate his wisdom to anthropologist Joseph E. Brown, which resulted in The Sacred Pipe. Who was this subject of an important oral autobiography transcribed by Nebraska poet John G. Neihardt?

John Mildenhall, a representative of the East India Company, arrived at Agra during his reign, but received no concession until the rule of Jahangir. It was hidden under floorboards, buried with an orphan, and given to a servant after it was shot. It was played in a monastery, a gypsy camp, in an English concert hall, and during intercourse. Its enactment was directly related to the impasse that followed the arrest of Thomas Darnel and four of his companions a year earlier. It was officially convoked by Count Gyula Andrassy, and the Italian representative was Count Luigi Corti, whose blunders would lead to his resignation. Laetus, his Prefect; Eclectus, his chamberlain; and Marcia, his mistress, could not kill him with poison, though they did engineer his death on New Year's Eve. After losing his fortune, this man served as governor of the Arizona territory from 1878 to 1883. His early exploits included an elopement with Jessie, daughter of Senator Thomas Hart Benton. One of its sponsors explained his reasons for backing it in his autobiography Fighting Liberal. Years after its beginning, the Southern and Northern Courts were unified for the first time with the end of the reign of Emperor Godaigo. As punishment for suspected dealings with the Persians and for conspiring to seize power in Sparta by a helot uprising, this man was walled up in the Temple of Athena and starved to death. The son of King Cleombrotus, he acted as regent for the son of Leonidas after the latter's death and served the Greeks well in the Persian Wars, commanding them in their victory at Plataea and capture of Byzantium. For 10 points name this Spartan, also the name of the first century geographer and author of a Description of Greece.

On the night of June 3, 1943, eleven sailors on shore leave stated that they were attacked by a group of Mexicans, and in response, a group of over 200 uniformed sailors chartered 20 cabs and charged into the heart of the Mexican American community in East Los Angeles, intent on mayhem. The specific objects of their rage were any person wearing a style of clothing associated with Mexicans and criminal behavior, and this violence continued over several days until the Navy intervened put a stop to it. Such are the actual, rather unpleasant events known by, what name, also the title of a song by the Cherry Poppin' Daddies?

This dynasty began its rule when its founder, Gustav Eriksson, successfully revolted against Christian II in 1523 and crowned himself Gustav I. Born around 460 BC, this Athenian was related to Miltiades through his father Olorus and as the owner of a gold mine in Thrace was a member of the aristocracy. Elected strategos in 424 BC, he failed to prevent the capture of the port of Amphipolis by the Spartan admiral Brasidas and was banished from Athens for the next 20 years, time which he used to observe the war from both sides. The daughter of a prominent painter, this woman was apprenticed under Gustav Kilmt but turned away from painting to music, studying composition under Alexander von Zemlinsky. For 10 points name this woman, whose amatory exploits are celebrated by Tom Lehrer.

This English statesman put into effect the Act of Supremacy and the dissolution of the monasteries during the 1530s, having earlier become agent and secretary to Cardinal Wolsey. The subject of the Supreme Court case Luther v. Borden, this insurrection began with the organization of the People's Party, which called a convention, adopted a new state constitution, and elected its leader as governor. Prior to this battle, Lutzingen was held by the Elector of Bavaria, while Marshal Tallard occupied the titular village. After marching down the Rhine, the British forces joined those of Eugene of Savoy, and on August 13 the Austrians defeated the forces of the Eelctor, while Tallard was forced to surrender to the Duke of Marlborough. This politician served as a Democratic Representative from 1909-15, and as alien property custodian during World War I. Known as the "fighting Quaker", assassination attempts aimed at John D. Rockefeller, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and himself prompted him to launch a November 1919 dragnet resulting in the arrest of 650 anarchist agitators, which was followed two months later by the arrest of 2,700 suspected Communists in 33 cities. This Supreme Court case ruled unconstitutional the same case which had been upheld in Tileston v. Ullman and Poe v. Ullman. From 1974-79, he was NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe. Before that he served as chief of staff for Nixon in the late stages of Watergate. A secondary focus of the movie Matinee as well as a forthcoming Kevin Costner film, the first proposal to resolve this incident was sent by telegram on October 26. This city lay at the junction of the Coosawattee [ku-sa-WAT-ee] and Conasauga [co-na-SAW-ga] rivers in present-day Gordon Conty, Georgia. By 1830 it had 50 residents and a main street 60 feet wide. Created as the territorial endowment of the descendents of Juchi, its capital was originally Sarai Batu, and later Sarai Berke. The aggressors had no cavalry, the decisive imbalance in this battle, which took place nine years after a revolt by the Ionian cities. His traveling party included 60,000 retainers and hundreds of camels so laden with treasure that they lowered the price of precious metals in Cairo. This Chicago native, a graduate of the University of Illinois-Chicago and the University of Chicago Law School, was elected to the Illinois State Legislature in 1978, serving there for nine years, and was the first African-American to serve as that body's assistant majority leader. Who was this first black woman senator who lost in her 1998 bid to be re-elected?

The Roman general at this battle unwisely decided to pursue the enemy rather than wait for Geminus who was moving to join him. Born off the coast of Jamaica, the son of merchant captain, he joined the East India Company at age 14. By age 30 he was the governor of Java, although in 1816 he was recalled to London. Graduating from the University of Oregon in 1975, he found it difficult to find a job before he accepted a position at The Advocate. Initially, the prospects for this Jacobite rebellion were promising, but the late arrival of James Edward Stuart to Scotland, the untimely death of French King Louis XIV, who had promised aid, and the vigor of the English government doomed the uprising. An earlier version was commissioned around 600 BC, and an architect named Chersiphron was hired to execute the project. Born Cheng, he might have been the son of the intriguing minister Lu Pu-Wei, rather than of Prince Chuang Hsiang of Ch'in. It overlooks Hechingen, a Baden-W?rttemberg city in the Swabian Alps, southwest of T?bingen. This Frenchman was a notable historian whose works included History of the French Revolution and History of the Consulate and the Empire, but he is better known for his role in public life. Born in Columbus, Ohio in 1890, his books include Seven Came Through and Fighting the Flying Circus. In 1942, this man and his newly established civil rights organization implemented the Gandhi-inspired tactic of nonviolent civil disobedience in Chicago, putting it into practice 14 years before Dr. King's Montgomery Bus Boycott. Born in about 1588 in present-day Connecticut, he was actually a Pequot. Who, unlike his namesake of Fenimore Cooper fictional fame, was the first chief of the Mohegans?
